Electrical discharge machining studies that specifically address Hastelloy indicate a marked sensitivity of process outcomes to the tool electrode material and its microstructure. Experimental comparisons using POCO graphite grades show that coarser graphite grains increase material removal rate (MRR) but at the cost of higher relative tool wear rate (TWR), whereas finer-grained graphite produces lower surface roughness (Ra). (Nowicki et al. 2022) The same trend (improved efficiency and reduced wear with fine-grained graphite) was independently reported when EDM of Hastelloy C-22 was performed with negative polarity, and the authors linked detached graphite grains to instability in discharges and altered process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across the reviewed EDM literature the principal electrical variables controlling MRR and Ra are peak current (amperage) and pulse duration (pulse-on time), with discharge current often accounting for the largest fraction of variance in MRR and roughness metrics. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nas & Kara 2022) Studies on other difficult-to-machine alloys similarly identify current and pulse duration as dominant factors for TWR and surface deterioration, and experimental optimisation methods such as Taguchi and ANOVA are commonly applied to quantify these effects. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Efforts to reduce TWR and improve dimensional accuracy in EDM use two broad strategies: modifying the electrode/workpiece physical state and altering the machining environment. Cryogenic treatment and process modifications such as powder-mixed dielectric or ultrasonic assistance are reported to change MRR, TWR and surface integrity by affecting thermal and electrical behaviours during sparking; meta-analyses of such associative techniques highlight their potential to mitigate the traditional trade-offs of EDM (high TWR, low MRR, coarse Ra). (Shastri et al. 2022)(Sana et al. 2024) For electrodes specifically, treating or alloying electrode materials (example: treated brass) has produced large reductions in electrode wear in other workpieces, indicating electrode processing can be an effective route to lower EWR. (Sana et al. 2024)

The literature also shows that EDM can be used for surface modification, electrical discharge coating (EDC), introducing the possibility that electrode composition and deposited layers interact to affect surface integrity and coating characteristics. (Liew et al. 2020) Studies on geometrical outcomes (for example square-hole machining of Hastelloy B2) emphasise that current and pulse duration not only drive wear rates but also change electrode geometry during machining, with sharp edges becoming rounded under unstable spark conditions. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Despite these findings, comparative data for copper electrodes and for engineered composite electrodes when machining Hastelloy alloys are not present in the assembled sources. [[NEEDS SOURCE: composite electrode studies for Hastelloy]]

###

(Nowicki et al. 2022)reports that, in EDM of Hastelloy C-22 with POCO graphite electrodes, the coarser-grained graphite (S-180, 10 µm) produced higher material removal rates but also greater relative tool wear, while the finer-grained graphite (AF-5, 1 µm) gave the lowest surface roughness; the study identified discharge current and pulse duration as the main drivers of MRR and Ra, and the time interval as the dominant factor for relative tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

(Nowicki et al. 2024)finds that using fine-grained graphite in negative-polarity EDM of Hastelloy C-22 raises process efficiency and lowers tool wear, and that graphite grain detachment alters spark stability and process effectiveness; the authors produced mathematical models linking grain size and machining parameters to MRR, relative TWR, and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

(Nas & Kara 2022)shows that, for a corrosion-resistant superalloy tested under varied pulse-on times (300–500 μs) and peak currents (6 and 10 A), peak current dominated both average surface roughness and MRR in ANOVA (74.79% and 86.43% influence, respectively), and Taguchi–gray relational analysis identified cryogenic treatment, pulse-on time and peak current as key factors for combined Ra and MRR performance. (Nas & Kara 2022)

(Ramabalan et al. 2024)measured EDM of Hastelloy B2 and observed that current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode wear, producing rapid rounding of square-electrode edges into hemispherical ends because unstable sparks and heat diffusion remove sharp features. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)similarly quantifies amperage as the overwhelmingly dominant factor for MRR and TWR in titanium EDM experiments, reporting percentage contributions from ANOVA that place amperage above other factors for multiple performance metrics. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

(Shastri et al. 2022)summarizes that researchers apply various auxiliary methods (cryogenic treatment, cryogenic cooling, powder-mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance) to reduce high TWR, low MRR and poor surface quality inherent to EDM, and it evaluates these associations against measures such as MRR, TWR, surface integrity and recast layer. (Shastri et al. 2022) Experimental results for brass electrodes in nanopowder-mixed and cryogenically treated conditions demonstrate large reductions in electrode wear rate and improvements in dimensional accuracy when deionized water or kerosene are used as dielectrics, with cryogenic treatment providing the largest EWR decreases reported in that study. (Sana et al. 2024)

(Liew et al. 2020)reviews electrical discharge coating (EDC) as a related process that deposits hard coatings via discharges and summarizes key EDC parameters and coating characteristics, implying a potential route to modify surface properties produced by discharge-based processes. (Liew et al. 2020)

###

Studies that directly compare electrode materials in EDM of nickel-based alloys focus predominantly on graphite and on process parameters that govern both material removal rate (MRR) and tool wear rate (TWR). Experimental work on Hastelloy C-22 shows that graphite electrode grain size substantially alters machining outcomes: coarser-grained graphite yields higher MRR but also increases relative tool wear, whereas finer-grained graphite produces lower surface roughness and, in later work, is reported to increase process efficiency while reducing tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Multiple investigations identify the same set of machining variables as primary drivers of MRR, TWR and surface finish. For EDM of Hastelloy, discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration emerge repeatedly as the dominant factors controlling MRR and Ra, while the interval between pulses (time off) is particularly influential for relative tool wear of graphite electrodes. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) In a factorial study that included cryogenic treatments, peak current accounted for the largest share of variance in both MRR and average surface roughness, consistent with the central role of current in thermal removal mechanisms. (Nas & Kara 2022)

Work on other nickel alloys reinforces the sensitivity of electrode geometry and wear to current and pulse duration: experiments on Hastelloy B2 reported that higher current and longer pulses substantially affect electrode taper, end radius and wear length, often rounding sharp electrode features into hemispherical ends through unstable sparking and heat diffusion. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) More generally, literature reviews of EDM note that the method’s main limitations are elevated TWR, low MRR relative to some processes, and degraded surface integrity from persistent sparking; reviewers compile various mitigation strategies such as cryogenic treatment, cryogenic cooling, powder-mixed dielectrics, and ultrasonic assistance to address these problems. (Shastri et al. 2022)

Alternate process variants and electrode treatments show promise for reducing wear or improving surface outcomes. Nanopowder-mixed EDM combined with cryogenic-treated electrodes produced substantial reductions in electrode wear rate and overcut for aluminium and brass electrodes in the reviewed experiments, illustrating how dielectric additives and electrode conditioning can change EWR and dimensional accuracy. (Sana et al. 2024) Electrical discharge coating (EDC) is presented as a related technique to modify surface characteristics or deposit hard coatings via discharges, offering another route to tailor surface integrity after EDM. (Liew et al. 2020)

Despite these findings, comparative data for copper electrodes on Hastelloy are not presented in the sourced literature. Similarly, the literature supplied contains no direct experimental comparisons involving composite electrodes on Hastelloy. [[NEEDS SOURCE: comparative data for composite electrodes on Hastelloy]]

### Electrical discharge machining performance with fine- and coarse-grained graphite electrodes

Nowicki et al. 2022 report that graphite with larger grains yields higher material removal rate but also produces greater relative tool wear when machining Hastelloy C-22 with EDM. (Nowicki et al. 2022) 
Their experiments compared POCO AF-5 (1 µm) and S-180 (10 µm) graphite and identified discharge current and pulse duration as the principal controls of MRR and Ra for both graphites, while the time interval (pulse-off) dominated relative tool wear of the graphite electrode. (Nowicki et al. 2022) 
The same pair of graphite grades was studied again by Nowicki et al. 2024 under negative polarity, where fine-grained POCO AF-5 increased process efficiency and reduced tool wear compared with coarse-grained EDM-180. (Nowicki et al. 2024) 
That study additionally observed that detached graphite grains alter discharge stability and thereby affect process efficiency, and it produced mathematical models linking machining parameters to MRR, relative TWR and Ra for Hastelloy C-22. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

### Process factors driving MRR, TWR and surface quality across studies

Peak current is reported as the dominant single parameter for both MRR and average surface roughness in the Taguchi/ANOVA analysis performed on a corrosion-resistant superalloy: it accounted for 86.43% of variance in MRR and 74.79% in Ra in Nas & Kara 2022. (Nas & Kara 2022) 
Akincioglu 2022 likewise found amperage (current) to be the most influential factor on MRR and TWR in EDM of titanium, with percentages near or above 99% in their ANOVA results. (Akıncıoğlu 2022) 
Ramabalan et al. 2024 show that current and pulse duration significantly affect electrode wear morphology during machining of Hastelloy B2, producing transformation of sharp square-electrode ends into hemispherical shapes under unstable sparking. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) 
Shastri et al. 2022 synthesise a range of mitigation strategies (cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed EDM, ultrasonic assistance) aimed at reducing high TWR, low MRR and poor surface integrity commonly observed in EDM processes. (Shastri et al. 2022)

### Alternative electrode and process interventions reported

Cryogenic treatment of workpieces and electrodes appears in experimental programmes: Nas & Kara 2022 identify an optimal combination including shallow cryogenic treatment, low pulse-on time and low peak current for combined Ra and MRR objectives in their Taguchi-gray analysis. (Nas & Kara 2022) 
Nanopowder in the dielectric together with electrode cryogenic treatment was reported to lower electrode wear and overcut for brass electrodes in a study using ANN-MOGA optimisation, with cryogenically treated brass showing the largest reductions in EWR and dimensional error when deionized water was used as the dielectric. (Sana et al. 2024) 
Liew et al. 2020 review electrical discharge coating (EDC) as a route to modify surface properties via discharges, summarising process parameters and coating characteristics relevant where surface integrity or new surface functions are targeted. (Liew et al. 2020)

Selective laser melting (SLM) produces near‑fully dense metallic parts by layerwise laser melting of powder, and the process intrinsically generates unique, fine microstructures through very high cooling rates. (Yap et al. 2015)(Haghdadi et al. 2020) The rapid thermal cycles in SLM act as an "in situ" heat treatment that promotes hierarchical (sub)grain structures and fine precipitates, features that distinguish additively manufactured steels from conventionally produced counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Studies on 18Ni‑300 (grade 300) maraging steel fabricated by SLM report an as‑built microstructure dominated by a very fine martensitic matrix and extremely small grains, consistent with cooling rates on the order of $10^7\ \mathrm{K/s}$. (Tan et al. 2018) Electron microscopy shows abundant needle‑shaped nanoprecipitates of Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) embedded in the martensite, which are implicated in age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Other work characterises the as‑printed condition of SLM maraging steel as a fine‑grained martensitic structure with relatively high surface roughness and no strong crystallographic texture across orthogonal sections. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) These as‑built features (fine martensite, submicron grain size, and pre‑existing nanoscale precipitates) explain the high strength but can contribute to reduced ductility without appropriate post‑processing. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Post‑processing modifies those microstructural states: heat treatments relieve residual stresses, promote precipitation strengthening, and can be combined with thermo‑chemical treatments. (Tan et al. 2018) Aging produces a maximum in nano‑hardness and correlates with precipitation evolution, while solution treatments and aging influence the response to subsequent nitriding. (Tan et al. 2018) In one study, plasma nitriding performed at $520\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for 6 h produced a compound layer whose integrity depended on prior heat treatment; nitriding without prior aging induced cracks in the nitride layer, whereas nitriding after prior heat treatment improved both wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated additive counterparts. (Godec et al. 2021) The combination of SLM’s intrinsic thermal history and controlled post‑treatments therefore governs the balance between mechanical strengthening and surface integrity after thermo‑chemical processing. (Tan et al. 2018)(Godec et al. 2021)

Reversed austenite formed by intercritical tempering has a measurable effect on chloride‑induced corrosion. (Khan et al. 2022) Khan et al. tempered SLM maraging steel at intercritical temperatures near $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to induce austenite reversion along martensite lath boundaries and found that the reversed austenite was associated with local Ni enrichment and improved pitting resistance in $3.5\ \mathrm{wt}\%$ NaCl: higher pitting potentials and lower corrosion current densities were reported for the $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$‑tempered specimens compared with as‑printed, aged, and homogenized samples. (Khan et al. 2022) Comparisons between SLM and wrought maraging steel after heat treatment show similar nano‑hardness and corrosion behaviour in the studied heat‑treated states, with precipitation playing a primary role in both hardness and corrosion potential; electropolishing can substantially reduce surface roughness and thereby affect measured corrosion responses. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018)
rows.b:
Tan et al. observe an average submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu\text{m}$ in SLM 300 maraging steel, implying cooling rates up to $10^7\ \text{K/s}$ in the as-fabricated material. (Tan et al. 2018) This rapid solidification produces a martensitic matrix containing dense, needle-shaped Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) nanoprecipitates that account for age hardening, and it also generates residual stress and building-orientation anisotropy; subsequent heat treatments both promote precipitation that strengthens the material and reduce residual stress while partially alleviating anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018)

Ahmadkhaniha et al. report a fine-grained martensitic microstructure in as-printed maraging steel with a surface roughness $R_a\approx 10\ \mu\text{m}$ and no detectable preferred texture across xy, xz and yz sections. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Their measurements show aging produces the maximum nano-hardness and the lowest corrosion potential among the tested conditions, and they attribute both hardness and corrosion behaviour primarily to precipitation phenomena; electropolishing reduced $R_a$ by about 65\%. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) These findings indicate that surface condition and precipitation state co-control both mechanical and electrochemical responses in SLM maraging steel. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Khan et al. find that an intercritical temper at $720\ ^\circ\text{C}$ produces reversed austenite that localises mainly along martensite-lath boundaries via Ni enrichment from dissolved intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) Electrochemical testing in $3.5\ \text{wt}\%$ NaCl shows the $720\ ^\circ\text{C}$-tempered specimens possess a higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, or homogenized samples lacking reversed austenite, so the study concludes that reversed austenite improves pitting resistance in chloride media. (Khan et al. 2022) Khan et al. also note that, before their work, the effect of martensite-to-austenite reversion on corrosion had been insufficiently understood. (Khan et al. 2022)

Godec et al. report that plasma nitriding performed without prior aging produces cracks in the compound nitride layer, whereas nitriding applied after appropriate prior heat treatments yields improved wear and corrosion resistance in SLM 18Ni-300 relative to untreated AM counterparts. (Godec et al. 2021) Together with broader reviews of SLM, these studies indicate that the AM process itself induces in situ thermal histories and precipitate distributions that strongly interact with subsequent heat- and thermochemical treatments to determine corrosion performance. (Godec et al. 2021)(Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Selective laser melting (SLM) builds metallic parts by layerwise laser melting and fusion of powder, producing near-net-shape components with relative densities approaching 99.9% under optimized conditions. (Yap et al. 2015) The layerwise thermal cycling and high local cooling rates in laser powder bed fusion create microstructures and precipitate states that differ from conventionally processed steels and can enhance properties such as strength, wear and corrosion resistance while posing challenges for ductility and fatigue. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

In the as-built condition, SLM maraging steel exhibits an extremely fine martensitic structure consistent across build sections and without a pronounced crystallographic texture. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) High cooling rates during SLM produce very small submicron grains (reported average $0.31\ \mu\text{m}$) and promote the formation of dense arrays of needle-shaped nanoprecipitates of Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) within the martensitic matrix, features that underpin the material’s age-hardening response. (Tan et al. 2018) Surface finish in the as-printed state can be relatively coarse (reported Ra ≈ 10 µm) but may be changed substantially by post-processing such as electropolishing. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Post-build thermal treatments alter both the fine-scale precipitate state and residual stress. Systematic aging informed by detected phase-transformation temperatures produces extensive Ni$_3$X precipitation that increases hardness and relieves residual stresses, and reduces build-orientation mechanical anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018) Thermochemical routes applied after SLM, such as plasma nitriding, interact with the prior heat-treatment condition: nitriding without prior aging produced defects in the compound layer, whereas nitriding of specimens that had been heat treated improved wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated additive-manufactured counterparts. (Godec et al. 2021) The AM process itself can act as an intrinsic heat treatment, causing in situ tempering and precipitation phenomena that influence the final microstructure and properties. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Intercritical tempering that induces martensite-to-austenite reversion (reversed austenite) has been linked to changes in corrosion performance in chloride media. In SLM maraging steel tempered within the $\alpha' + \gamma$ range (example: 720°C), reversed austenite nucleates preferentially at martensite lath boundaries where local Ni enrichment occurs, and specimens with such reversed austenite exhibited higher pitting potentials, lower corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rates in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as-printed, conventionally aged, or homogenized samples without reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022) More generally, precipitation state governs both hardness and electrochemical behaviour: aging that maximizes nano-hardness also shifts corrosion potential, indicating that precipitate evolution strongly affects corrosion response. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)
rows.b:
Tan et al. report an average submicron grain size of $0.31\ \mu$m in SLM 18Ni-300 maraging steel, indicating cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$ during fabrication. (Tan et al. 2018) This high cooling rate produces a fine martensitic matrix containing dense, needle-shaped Ni3X precipitates that form in situ and contribute to age hardening; microscopy in that study resolved interfacial relationships between precipitates and the matrix and linked strengthening to Orowan and coherency-strain mechanisms. (Tan et al. 2018) Haghdadi et al. synthesize findings across AM steels and attribute such hierarchical subgrain structures and fine precipitates to the unique thermal cycles of laser powder bed fusion, noting that these microstructural features often yield higher strength and modified corrosion behaviour relative to conventionally produced steels. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Ahmadkhaniha et al. find that as-printed SLM maraging steel exhibits a fine-grained martensitic structure with a surface roughness $Ra\approx 10\ \mu$m and no strong crystallographic texture across three orthogonal sections. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) In their comparison, nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour of heat-treated SLM specimens and conventionally wrought maraging steel are similar, and aging produces the highest nano-hardness while lowering corrosion potential; the study identifies precipitation as the principal factor controlling both hardness and corrosion response. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Yap et al. describe SLM as capable of producing near-full-density parts (up to 99.9% relative density) through layerwise laser melting and rapid solidification, which underpins the dense microstructures observed in these experimental reports. (Yap et al. 2015)

Khan et al. report that tempering in the intercritical $\alpha' + \gamma$ range at $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ produces reversed austenite that precipitates primarily along martensite-lath boundaries in SLM maraging steel, a process promoted by local nickel enrichment from dissolving intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) That study measured electrochemical behaviour in $3.5\ \mathrm{wt}\%$ NaCl and found the $720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ tempered specimens show a higher pitting potential, reduced corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rate compared with as-printed, aged, and homogenized specimens lacking reversed austenite; the authors conclude that reversed austenite improves pitting resistance. (Khan et al. 2022)

Godec et al. examined plasma nitriding applied to SLM 18Ni-300 after varied prior heat treatments and observed that nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound layer, whereas nitriding following prior heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance of the additive-manufactured material. (Godec et al. 2021) Yan et al. compared SLM and cold-spray composites and showed SLM yields higher densification and lower porosity, factors that influence both mechanical behaviour and likely surface-controlled corrosion processes. (Yan et al. 2018) Afkhami et al. and Haghdadi et al. highlight remaining gaps: although AM induces in situ tempering and precipitation that modify corrosion response, acceptable ductility and fatigue remain challenges and the interplay between microstructural anisotropy, heat treatment routes, and chloride-induced corrosion is not comprehensively mapped. (Afkhami et al. 2019)(Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Household decisions about rooftop photovoltaic (PV) adoption are strongly shaped by financial considerations: initial capital outlay and perceptions of running costs form persistent inhibitors. Empirical analyses identify upfront cost and expected maintenance burden as negative influences on willingness to adopt, with cost often appearing as a primary barrier in survey-based studies. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021)

A nationally representative analysis from Uganda shows that loan- or installment-style payment options increase uptake of larger solar home systems relative to one-time purchase, implying that flexible finance converts constrained demand into actual adoption. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Parsad et al. likewise report that subsidies reduce initial investment risk and operate as a key financial motivator in Indian household decisions. (Parsad et al. 2020)

Policy instruments and subsidy design therefore play an outsized role in shaping household investor behavior, both by lowering up-front risk and by signaling governmental support. Indian policy goals and targets frame these incentives: national targets for solar capacity position rooftop PV as a deliberate element of the renewable portfolio, and analyses of Indian policy instruments link these targets to the broader effort to expand rooftop deployment. (Goel 2016)(J & Majid 2020) Specific pilot implementations also reveal gaps between policy intent and on-the-ground uptake, indicating that incentives alone do not guarantee diffusion. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Non-financial constraints interact with financial barriers: limited technical knowledge, weak awareness, and perceived risks reduce adoption even where subsidies or finance are available. Parsad et al. find that technical barriers and deficits in awareness remain significant predictors of investment decisions, and that non-financial motivators such as environmental concern operate alongside but do not fully substitute for clear information and trust in the technology. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021) Field surveys in pilot projects underscore user-experience issues and information gaps about site suitability and system performance as impediments to uptake. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Equity and spatial patterns further complicate adoption dynamics: research warns that growth in household solar can produce uneven outcomes across demographic and geographic groups, so that expanding deployment without attention to distributional effects risks reinforcing inequities. (Sovacool et al. 2022) At the same time, country-level reviews highlight infrastructural and institutional constraints that shape the feasibility of scaling rooftop PV, meaning that technical potential alone does not resolve barriers embedded in governance, market structure, and program implementation. (Khare et al. 2013)(J & Majid 2020)
rows.b:
Parsad et al. 2020 find that government subsidies are the primary motivator that helps households overcome the initial investment risk for rooftop PV, and that low purchase prices and low maintenance costs further strengthen the financial case for adoption. (Parsad et al. 2020) Paring structural-equation outputs with an artificial neural network, they report that technical barriers and gaps in knowledge and awareness also significantly forecast investment decisions, indicating that policy support interacts with informational and technical constraints. (Parsad et al. 2020)

Aarakit et al. 2021 find that affordability governs which solar products households choose: flexible payment mechanisms increase uptake of more expensive solar home systems and kits, while rural residence and income predict the type of system adopted. (Aarakit et al. 2021) From this they infer that absence of payment flexibility constrains poorer households from selecting higher-capacity rooftop solutions. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Tanveer et al. 2021 similarly report that perceived cost negatively affects willingness to adopt household PV, while perceived benefits and self-efficacy increase willingness. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Kappagantu et al. 2015 report survey evidence from a smart-grid pilot in Puducherry showing that users raise questions about available roof space, experience with the technology, and practical installation concerns. (Kappagantu et al. 2015) Parsad et al. 2020 identify technical barriers alongside knowledge and awareness deficits as significant inhibitors in household decision models, suggesting that practical site constraints and limited user familiarity reduce adoption propensity. Mobile diabetes self-management apps show mixed evidence for improving glycaemic control, while patterns of engagement and specific design features emerge as central determinants of sustained use. A pragmatic multisite randomized trial of the BlueStar app found no overall difference in HbA1c between intervention and control arms at three months, although exploratory analysis within users linked greater daily app use to modest reductions in HbA1c; usage varied markedly between clinical sites, indicating contextual influences on engagement. Smaller or pilot studies similarly report behavior-level gains without demonstrated glycaemic benefit within short evaluations. A 12-week pilot of an app for adolescents with diabetes increased the frequency of blood glucose monitoring by 50% and achieved high user satisfaction, but the authors stated that demonstrating changes in HbA1c would require larger, longer trials and interventions that tie incentives to decision-making as well as measurement. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Taken together, these findings indicate that increased self-monitoring or other proximal behaviours can be achieved, yet translation into HbA1c improvement is not consistently observed within the durations studied. Practical and market realities also shape sustained engagement. Reviews of app ecosystems highlight concerns about variable app quality, the need for certification or vetting, and the importance of matching content to users’ health and digital literacy to avoid harmful or ineffective tools. (Boulos et al. 2014) Comparative app audits report that many commercial diabetes apps emphasize logging and reminders rather than tailored education or therapeutic guidance, suggesting a mismatch between common app features and the educational or decision-support elements users and clinicians request.
